name: Sulisobenzone

lead: Sulisobenzone (benzophenone-4) is a UV filter that absorbs UVB and short UVA. Unlike other benzophenones it dissolves in water, so it also appears in some hair products.
Most published work on it concerns its presence in rivers and wastewater rather than human trials.

paras: It absorbs ultraviolet light through its benzophenone structure; the sulfonic acid group makes it water-soluble.
Sources reviewed contain no dedicated human safety trials. Environmental studies report it in surface water, and UV filters as a class have been tested for hormone-like activity in cells and fish.

lead: Sulisobenzone, or benzophenone-4, is a water-soluble benzophenone UV filter that protects against UVB and short-wave UVA light.[1] Its sodium salt is called benzophenone-5.[1] It is used in some sunscreens and, per its cosmetic ingredient listing, in hair products to protect colour and structure.[1]

Wikipedia's entry is a stub covering chemistry and uses only.[1] Research on sulisobenzone is mostly environmental: it has been among the most abundant UV filters detected in Swiss river water, and fish and cell assays have examined hormone-like activity of UV filters.[2][3] The North American Contact Dermatitis Group has also included UV-filter allergens in its patch-test series.[4]

paras: Sulisobenzone has a molar mass of about 308 g/mol and melts at about 145 C.[1] The sulfonic acid group makes it far more water-soluble than other benzophenones.[1]

It is an ingredient in some sunscreens where it absorbs UVB and UVA.[1] Wikipedia groups it among UVA+UVB filters approved by one or more agencies (such as the US FDA, EU SCCS and Australia's TGA) without detailing specific approvals.[1]

A Swiss monitoring study found BP-4 occurred at the highest concentrations among four detected UV filters downstream of wastewater plants.[2] Other studies have assessed UV filters in surface waters across several countries and in wastewater treatment, and compared in vitro and fish estrogenic activity of filters.[3][5]
No studies found of sulisobenzone as a treatment. Related clinical data include a North American patch-test report that covers UV-filter allergens.[4]
